messages.body_plain:
Dear Professors,

I ask to forgive for my English language, and I hope you understand me.
In using a replication example I was wanting to be certain about my solutions and compare the results from both packages, by using the data called "d.partybans".

The complex solutions and the most parsiomonious solutions are the same, except for the intermediate solution that it is different and I don't know why.

I use this code:

library(QCApro)
data(d.partybans)
eQMC(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", exo.facs = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1))

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}

p.sol: C{0} + C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + F{0}*T{2} + F{1}*V{0}

M1:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*V{0}) => PB{1}
M2:    C{1}*F{1} + C{1}*F{2} + F{2}*T{2} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{0}*F{2}*T{1} + C{2}*T{1}*V{0} +
       C{2}*T{2}*V{0} + (C{1}*T{0}) => PB{1}

And then I compare this solutions with what I obtained from the other package QCA:

library(QCA)
minimize(d.partybans, outcome = "PB{1}", conditions = c("C", "F", "T", "V"), include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, "1;2", 2, 1), all.sol = TRUE)

>From C1P1:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + T{2}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} -> PB{1}

>From C1P2:

M1:    C{1} + F{2} + T{1}*V{0} + C{0}*F{1}*T{2} + C{2}*T{2}*V{0} -> PB{1}

I was expected to see similar but I see very, very different solutions. I then show this to one colleague and he said to ask on this help list. Kindly ask you to explain why I get so different solutions.

Thank you so much,
Dmitri

PS: forgive me for second email, I was wrong with one email address

Dear Dmitri,

I am currently at the American QCA conference in Los Angeles, to responding a bit slow.
If I remember correctly, the issue you are experiencing  is due to a bug that has been solved a long time ago in the main package QCA, and which is still present in the QCApro copy package of that old version.

This means that QCApro is practically obsolete. I am not sure if you prefer to produce all possible solutions or simply used the default minimal disjunctively in package QCApro, but given that package QCA also produces those my advice is to simply stop using that package. I have my doubts the current maintainer has the necessary skills to patch that error.

And this is not the only problem that plagues that package. A much more serious one is that it cannot always guarantee a solution.

Consider this example:

set.seed(12345)
pichart <- matrix(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1825, prob = c(0.2, 0.8), replace = TRUE), ncol = 73)
QCApro::solveChart(pichart)

Dear Dimitri,

I am personally a big fan of Professor Dusa's work, particularly the QCA package and accompanying textbook. Many authors have discussed the importance of adopting QCA as an approach, not just a blunt instrument. It is my understanding that the parsimonious and conservative/complex solution types are analytical steps in calculating the intermediate solution and, while they should still be examined and considered, they are typically less desirable. Ragin summarises the common preference for the intermediate solution in Redesigning Social Inquiry (pg. 175) "In general, intermediate solutions are preferred because they are often the most interpretable. When limited diversity is substantial, complex solutions can be exceedingly intricate because little or no simplification occurs. Likewise, under these same conditions, parsimonious solutions can be unrealistically simple, due to the incorporation of many (easy and difficult) counterfactual combinations. Intermediate solutions strike a balance between parsimony and complexity, based on the substantive and theoretical knowledge of the investigator" (note I have added the bold here). Examining all three solutions in the context of this substantive and theoretical knowledge should not be overlooked. I encourage you to read Professor Dusa's article titled Critical Tension: Sufficiency and parsimony in QCA <https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124119882456>.

Kind Regards,
Alicia

>
> Thus, if you want to carry out serious configurational research, you should be extremely careful with QCA.

>
>

If you want to test a specific disjunction for being SUIN, I would create it by hand and feed it into the QCAfit() function. If there are multiple disjunctions or the SUIN analysis is exploratory, I suggest using superSubset() from the QCA package. You can negate the outcome with ~ and you can determine how many disjunctions you want to see by choosing the minimum level of consistency, coverage and ron.

Kind regards

Ingo

I concur to Ingo’s suggestion.
One analyses SUIN conditions mainly for necessity, in the same way that INUS conditions are analysed for sufficiency.

To add my 2 cents, I would recommend taking a look at the function pof() from package QCA.
Using this function, it is possible to actually test sufficiency and necessity by actually writing expressions, rather than creating the conditions prior to calculating the parameters of fit. It saves one step, and it is (in my opinion) more clear.

Something like:

pof(LIT + IND + STB <- SURV, data = LF)

               inclN   RoN   covN
----------------------------------
1         LIT  0.991  0.509  0.643
2         IND  0.669  0.786  0.684
3         STB  0.920  0.680  0.707
4  expression  1.000  0.367  0.587
----------------------------------

For the negation of the outcome you can use a tilde, as per Ingo’s suggestion:

pof(LIT + IND + STB <- ~SURV, data = LF)

               inclN   RoN   covN
----------------------------------
1         LIT  0.573  0.387  0.414
2         IND  0.354  0.661  0.403
3         STB  0.467  0.509  0.399
4  expression  0.711  0.309  0.464
----------------------------------

I hope this helps,
Adrian

I would warmly suggest reading the chapter on calibration that is freely available online, here:

It is my impression you are mixing up the method of "direct assignment”, which I’ve shown in the recode() command earlier, with the “direct method” of calibration, that is indeed using either three or six thresholds.

Direct method:
https://bookdown.org/dusadrian/QCAbook/calibration.html#s-shape

Please also note the function rob.calibrange() is not a calibration function. What it does is to find a range of thresholds for which the calibration seems to be robust. It is part of the add-on package SetMethods.

For the formal calibration function, with all necessary arguments, do have a look at the help page of the function:
?calibrate

I hope this helps,
Adrian

In the previous message where the email list was not in the recipients, you've sent an MRE which I was able to use and replicate your error. It seems to be due to a bug in package SetMethods (and I added there Nena Oana in the CC).

INNOV2added <- data.frame(
   row.names = c("Bulgaria16”, "Bulgaria18”, "Estonia16",

  highpatent = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0.67, 1),
     highinv = c(0.33, 0.33, 1, 1, 1, 1),
   highlinks = c(0, 0, 1, 0.67, 1, 0),
     highfdi = c(0.67, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1),
    highesif = c(0, 0.33, 0, 0.67, 0, 1),
    hightax2 = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0.67, 0.67),
     lowflow = c(0.33, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 0, 0)
)

T <- truthTable(
       data = INNOV2added,
       outcome = "highpatent",
       incl.cut = 0.8,
       pri.cut = 0.51,
       n.cut = 1,
       sort.by <http://sort.by> = "incl",
       show.cases = TRUE
)

solT <- minimize(input = T, details = TRUE)

pimplot(data = INNOV2added, outcome = "highpatent", results = solT)

Error in `[.data.frame`(results$tt$recoded.data, , outcome) :
  undefined columns selected

So that does yield an error. The fix is to rename all columns to uppercase:

names(INNOV2added) <- toupper(names(INNOV2added))

T2 <- truthTable(
       data = INNOV2added,
       outcome = "HIGHPATENT",
       incl.cut = 0.8,
       pri.cut = 0.51,
       n.cut = 1,
       sort.by <http://sort.by> = "incl",
       show.cases = TRUE
)

solT2 <- minimize(input = T2, details = TRUE)

pimplot(data = INNOV2added, outcome = "HIGHPATENT", results = solT2)

And this works as expected. The key to solve these kinds of errors is to check what is different in your example, compared with the example that actually works in the help file of the function pimplot(). This is how I figured out the only possible difference is the case sensitivity.

I hope this helps,
Adrian
